{"id": "d978470b-eb6d-4a86-8724-a322a1f692ac", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_84GUQeXsLoeOhW3Wm11gMz", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Quotas for the bedrock-runtime endpoint\",\"context\":\"## Requesting a quota increase\\n\\nThe steps for requesting a quota increase for your account depend on the value in the **Adjustable** column in the quotas table in Amazon Bedrock service quotas.\\n\\n**Important:**\\n\\nBefore requesting a quota increase, verify that the model is not in a *Legacy* or *Deprecated* lifecycle status. Quota increases are not granted for models that are scheduled for retirement. Check the model's lifecycle status on the Model lifecycle page and consider migrating to the successor model instead.\\n\\n* If a quota is marked as **Yes**, you can adjust it by following the steps at Requesting a Quota Increase in the Service Quotas User Guide.\\n* For any model, you can request an increase for the following quotas together:\\n\\n + Cross-Region InvokeModel tokens per minute for `${model}`\\n + On-demand InvokeModel tokens per minute for `${model}`\\n + Cross-Model Max Tokens Per Day\\n\\n To request an increase for any combination of these quotas, request an increase for the **Cross-Region InvokeModel tokens per minute for `${model}`** quota by following the steps at Requesting a Quota Increase in the Service Quotas User Guide. After you do so, the support team will reach out and offer you the option of also increasing the other two quotas.\\n\\n **Note:**\\n\\n Due to overwhelming demand, priority will be given to customers who generate traffic that consumes their existing quota allocation. Your request might be denied if you don't meet this condition.\\n\\nFor `bedrock-mantle` quota increases, see Requesting a quota increase\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-runtime.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot the \\\"ThrottlingException\\\" error when I use Amazon Bedrock on-demand resources?\",\"context\":\"### Request a quota increase\\n\\nNew AWS accounts might have lower initial quotas than the default quotas. Specific models have non-adjustable fixed quotas. If your workload traffic exceeds your account's on-demand quotas, then contact [AWS Support](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awssupport/latest/user/case-management.html#creating-a-support-case) or your account manager to [request a quota increase](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-increase.html). AWS might adjust default quotas based on usage patterns or service requirements.\\n\\nInclude the following information in your request:\\n\\n* The name of the quota to increase\\n* The model ID\\n* The Region for the quota increase\\n* A brief explanation of your use case\\n* Your projected usage, including steady and peak tokens and requests per minute, and average input and output tokens per request\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-throttling-error\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Optimize your applications for scale and reliability on Amazon Bedrock | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"#### Why token limits matter\\n\\nEven if your request count is modest, a single large prompt or a model that produces long outputs can consume thousands of tokens at once. Token\u2011based throttling occurs when the sum of input tokens, output tokens, and tokens reserved by `max_tokens` processed per minute exceeds your account\u2019s TPM quota for that model. Critically, if `max_tokens` is not explicitly set in your request, it defaults to the model\u2019s maximum output capacity (for example, 64,000 tokens for Claude Sonnet). This means a modest request can silently reserve far more quota than intended, and is a common cause of unexpected throttling. See section 3 below for the full quota lifecycle equations.\\n\\nFor example, if your application uses Claude Opus 4.6 with a default quota of 2,000,000 tokens per minute (TPM), and each request has 500 input tokens with `max_tokens` set to 1,000, Bedrock initially reserves 1,500 tokens per request from your quota (500 input + 1,000 `max_tokens`). That gives you a theoretical capacity of ~1,333 concurrent requests per minute (2M \u00f7 1,500). But if you leave max_tokens unset and it defaults to 64,000, the same request reserves 64,500 tokens, dropping your capacity to just ~31 concurrent requests per minute from the same 2M TPM quota.All major Bedrock models have TPM quotas ranging from 200K to 8M TPM depending on the model, with newer models like Claude Sonnet 4.6 offering 5M TPM. These quotas are adjustable through AWS Service Quotas, allowing you to request increases as your application scales.\\n\\n**What this looks like in practice**\\n\\nYou may notice that your application runs smoothly under normal workloads, but suddenly starts failing when users paste large documents, upload long transcripts, or run bulk summarization jobs. These are symptoms that token throughput, not request frequency, is the bottleneck. For bulk jobs, you should be using batch inference, which has separate quotas (up to 10,000 records per batch with a 24-hour processing window) and offers 50% reduced prices compared to on-demand inference\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/optimize-your-applications-for-scale-and-reliability-on-amazon-bedrock/\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Checking AWS docs on Bedrock quota increases for model throttling"}

{"id": "72ed3b24-bd1d-42b7-9924-7fe89ce2c7f4", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here's how to raise your Bedrock InvokeModel limits for Claude:

**1. Find the right quota in Service Quotas**
Go to Service Quotas → Amazon Bedrock → and look for the per-model quotas for your Claude model, specifically:
- **On-demand InvokeModel requests per minute** for the Claude model
- **On-demand InvokeModel tokens per minute** for the Claude model
- **Cross-Region InvokeModel tokens per minute** (if you're using cross-region inference profiles)

**2. Request the increase**
- If the quota shows **Adjustable: Yes**, you can request an increase directly in the Service Quotas console (or via `request-service-quota-increase` API).
- Requesting an increase on **Cross-Region InvokeModel tokens per minute** also lets AWS Support offer to raise the related **On-demand tokens per minute** and **Cross-Model Max Tokens Per Day** quotas together.
- Some models have **non-adjustable fixed quotas** — in that case you'd need to go through AWS Support/your account team instead.

**3. Include this info in your request** (improves approval odds):
- Quota name, model ID, and region
- Brief use case description
- Projected usage: steady-state and peak tokens/requests per minute, average input/output tokens per request

**One important gotcha before you request more quota:** if `max_tokens` isn't explicitly set in your InvokeModel calls, it defaults to the model's max output (e.g., 64,000 tokens for Claude Sonnet), which reserves far more quota per request than you'd expect and can cause throttling well before you're actually near your real usage. Setting `max_tokens` explicitly often resolves throttling without needing a quota increase at all.

Also worth noting: AWS prioritizes quota increase requests for accounts that are already consuming most of their existing allocation — so if you're nowhere near your current limit, the request may get denied.

Want me to check your current Bedrock quota values and recent throttling activity for the Claude model you're using, so we know whether this is really a quota ceiling versus a `max_tokens` issue?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
